strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: extends tool-augmented, multi-step agentic reasoning (as popularized by ReAct/OpenThinkIMG-style frameworks) into the geospatial/EO domain, which prior EO-VLMs (GeoChat, EarthDial) and even recent EO-agent works (ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, Geo-OLM) only partially cover, as clearly summarized in Table 1.

Substantial, well-organized dataset (14,538 train / 1,169 eval instances, >100K/7K reasoning steps) spanning RGB, SAR, GIS vector layers, and spectral indices (NDVI/NBR/NDBI), with a described automated curation and validation pipeline (Sample Sufficiency Filter, Annotation Harmonizer, deterministic tool-call replay) that adds a degree of quality control beyond typical instruction-tuning corpora.

A concretely specified unified tool registry (Table A2) covering perceptual, GIS, spectral, georeferenced-raster, and utility operations with a consistent JSON-based calling schema, which is a useful engineering contribution for reproducible agentic pipelines.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation: both step-by-step (tool-agnostic) and end-to-end (live execution) protocols, multiple complementary metrics (Inst./Tool/ArgN/ArgV/Summ, category-wise F1, tool-order fidelity at three strictness levels, task accuracy), plus supplementary error-type breakdowns and a model-backbone ablation (Qwen3-4B vs Qwen2.5-7B).

The fine-tuned 4B model shows consistent, sizable improvements over its own untuned baseline and over much larger open-source models, and is competitive with or exceeds frontier proprietary models (GPT-4o, o4-mini) on several structural/procedural metrics (tool selection, argument correctness, trajectory-order fidelity), which is a meaningful applied result given the modest parameter count.
Illustrative qualitative examples (Figs. 1, A1-A3) make the intended use cases and failure modes of baselines concrete and support the paper's motivating claims.
weaknesses: The data-generation pipeline for natural-language queries and reasoning trajectories relies on an unspecified 'structured LLM-driven module'; the exact generator model(s), prompting strategy, and the extent/nature of human verification (beyond GSD sanity checks on the test set) are not clearly described, which limits reproducibility and raises questions about potential synthetic biases or repetitive patterns in the trajectories.

Methodologically the core training contribution is standard supervised fine-tuning on curated trajectories (Eq. 2-3); the technical novelty is concentrated in dataset construction and tool-registry engineering rather than in the learning algorithm itself, which should be more explicitly framed (the paper is best read as a Dataset/Benchmark + Applied/Systems contribution rather than a new algorithmic method).

Several evaluation category subsets are small (e.g., only 123 index-based and 503 RGB/SAR queries in the 1,169-sample benchmark), which may limit the statistical robustness of category-wise comparisons (Fig. 7) and some F1 breakdowns.

Precise operational definitions of some metrics (e.g., exactly how Instance Accuracy or Summarization Accuracy are computed, and how the LLM-judge prompt in Fig. A5 handles edge cases beyond the examples shown) are only partially specified; combined with use of an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) for non-generative task accuracy, this introduces potential evaluation noise/bias that is not quantified (e.g., no inter-rater or judge-consistency check).

No explicit statement of dataset/code release, licensing of the underlying source datasets for redistribution (DOTA, xBD, FloodNet, OSM, GEE, etc.), or compute/training-run variance (single run, no seeds/repeats reported), which affects reproducibility claims.

Comparisons to frontier closed models (GPT-4o, o4-mini) are somewhat asymmetric since those models are not fine-tuned on the target distribution, so some of OpenEarthAgent's gains may partly reflect in-domain adaptation rather than a more general reasoning improvement; this should be discussed as a caveat.
Minor presentation issues remain, e.g., a broken cross-reference ('Table ??') in the Data Sources paragraph, indicating incomplete proofreading.

strengths: Comprehensive multimodal corpus (14,538 train / 1,169 test instances, 100K+ reasoning steps) spanning RGB, SAR, GIS, and spectral-index modalities across seven thematic domains, filling a genuine gap relative to prior EO benchmarks that largely lack explicit tool-grounded reasoning traces.

Well-engineered data curation pipeline with deterministic replay validation (executing candidate tool calls to verify argument correctness and geometric validity before inclusion), which is a meaningful step toward higher-quality supervision than purely LLM-generated trajectories.

Extensive empirical evaluation: both step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, comparison against a wide range of frontier (GPT-5, GPT-4o, o4-mini) and open-source baselines, plus a large supplementary suite of ablations (data composition, in-context learning vs. fine-tuning, tool-schema complexity, tool ordering, high-level planning, cross-benchmark evaluation on Earth-Agent, and LLM-judge robustness checks).

Demonstrates that a small (4B) fine-tuned model can match or exceed much larger frontier models on procedural correctness metrics (Inst./Tool/ArgN/ArgV) and trajectory-order fidelity, which is a practically useful and interesting finding for resource-constrained deployment.
Clear, modular tool-registry abstraction (perceptual, GIS, spectral, georeferenced-raster, utility tools) that is extensible without retraining, supporting reproducibility and reuse.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is primarily supervised fine-tuning on a curated trajectory corpus with a standardized tool schema; there is limited architectural or algorithmic novelty beyond this (no RL, no novel policy-learning mechanism), which somewhat narrows the technical contribution relative to the claims of a "unified agentic architecture."

Both the training data (queries + reasoning traces) and much of the evaluation (Summarization/Answer Accuracy via GPT-4o-mini as judge) are LLM-generated/LLM-judged, raising potential circularity and reliability concerns; the Qwen3-30B judge comparison helps but only shows rank preservation, not absolute calibration against human judgment beyond the test-set manual inspection.

Table 4 GIS F1 scores are near-saturated (>90%) for nearly all models including weak baselines, which is suspicious and suggests the GIS tool-selection task may be too easy/low-diversity to be discriminative, undermining the strength of claims about superior GIS reasoning.

No direct comparison against the actual Earth-Agent or ThinkGeo systems (only their backbone LLMs are compared within the authors' own framework), so it is unclear how OpenEarthAgent performs against these prior tool-augmented EO agents' own pipelines rather than re-implemented baselines.

The underlying imagery/annotation sources (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, etc.) are pre-existing benchmarks; the novelty rests on the synthesized queries/reasoning traces layered on top, and the paper does not discuss potential biases or artifacts introduced by the LLM-driven question/trace synthesis pipeline (e.g., template diversity, hallucinated reasoning steps that still execute correctly).

Limited discussion of failure cases or limitations of the approach itself (e.g., generalization to truly out-of-distribution geospatial tasks, tool registry scalability, robustness to real GIS/GeoTIFF edge cases) in the main text; most of this appears only in supplementary error analysis.
